by_task.when: Federal exemptions under 11 U.S.C. § 522(d) are allowable and the asset is property of the debtor.
by_task.procedure: Evaluate 11 U.S.C. § 522(d)(5) independently for every asset and include it even when a more specific federal exemption also applies. Its monetary ceiling limits protection but does not defeat EC eligibility.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not include § 522(d)(5) when federal subsection (d) exemptions are unavailable or the item is not the debtor's property.

by_task.when: Federal exemptions under 11 U.S.C. § 522(d) are allowable and the asset is debtor-owned property.
by_task.procedure:
For each asset, output one separate § 522(d)(5) alternative and retain every applicable specific federal alternative. The claim for the whole asset is always the lesser of its value and the applicable ceiling: § 522(d)(5) uses $15,425 for one debtor or $30,850 for jointly owned property of two joint debtors when both full ceilings are available. Apply the same lesser-of rule to specific provisions; never report a ceiling when the asset is worth less. Section 522(d)(3) is capped at $700 per item. For jointly owned jewelry of two joint debtors, § 522(d)(4) protects the lesser of the whole value and $3,750; its one-debtor ceiling is $1,875.
Execution example: For a hypothetical jointly owned vehicle worth $20,000, retain the vehicle citation at its own $4,450 ceiling and add § 522(d)(5) at $20,000. For a hypothetical low-value specific-category item, both its specific claim and wildcard claim must be limited to the item's value.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not use § 522(d)(5) when federal subsection (d) exemptions are unavailable or the asset is not debtor property. Do not omit it because another federal provision applies, substitute its amount for another provision, copy any ceiling above the asset's value, or duplicate a citation.

by_task.when: Pennsylvania exemptions are allowable and the asset is property of the judgment debtor.
by_task.procedure: Include 42 Pa. Cons. Stat. § 8123 as an independent general-property alternative, while retaining every applicable specific Pennsylvania or federal exemption.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not include § 8123 for property outside the debtor's interest or when Pennsylvania law is not an allowable namespace.

by_task.when: Pennsylvania exemptions are allowable and the asset is property of the judgment debtor.
by_task.procedure:
Make a separate § 8123 pass over every asset, including vehicles, household goods, jewelry, animals, clothing and business-use property. Add exactly one § 8123 entry without removing federal or specific Pennsylvania alternatives. For the whole asset, report the lesser of its value and $300 for one debtor, or the lesser of its value and $600 for jointly owned property when each spouse claims the exemption.
Execution example: A hypothetical jointly owned item worth $180 receives a § 8123 claim of $180, not $600; an item worth more than $600 receives $600.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not apply § 8123 outside the debtor's property or a Pennsylvania namespace. Do not replace it with the parent citation § 8124(a), copy its ceiling when the asset is worth less, or treat the absence of a specific Pennsylvania category as a reason to omit § 8123. Section 8124(a)(4) remains limited to a commissioned officer's or enlisted person's uniform and accoutrements.

by_task.when: Oregon exemptions are allowable and the asset is personal property of the debtor.
by_task.procedure: Include Or. Rev. Stat. § 18.345(1)(p) independently for the asset, without replacing applicable category-specific Oregon or federal exemptions.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not apply paragraph (p) to real property, property not belonging to the debtor, or a non-Oregon context.

by_task.when: Oregon exemptions are allowable and the asset is debtor-owned personal property.
by_task.procedure:
Add § 18.345(1)(p) as its own alternative even when another Oregon paragraph, § 18.362, or a federal provision also protects the item. Report the lesser of the whole asset's value and $400; do not automatically double this asset-level amount for joint debtors.
Execution example: For a hypothetical jacket worth $80, retain its wearing-apparel citation and add paragraph (p) at $80, not $400.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not apply paragraph (p) to real property, nondebtor property, or a non-Oregon context. A category-specific citation does not displace paragraph (p).

by_task.when: Illinois exemptions are allowable and the asset is debtor-owned personal property used for personal rather than business purposes.
by_task.procedure: Before evaluating specific Illinois subsections, make a separate pass over every asset satisfying this condition and include 735 Ill. Comp. Stat. 5/12-1001(b). Then evaluate specific subsections independently, retaining subsection (b) when subsection (a), (c), or another specific provision also applies; “other property” does not make these alternatives mutually exclusive for EC.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not apply subsection (b) to business-use property, non-personal property, or property outside the debtor's ownership.

by_task.when: Illinois exemptions are allowable and the asset is debtor-owned personal property used for personal rather than business purposes.
by_task.procedure:
Use two independent passes. First, add exactly one § 12-1001(b) entry to every such asset—including animals, clothing and property lacking a specific category—and report the lesser of whole-asset value and $4,000 for one debtor or $8,000 for jointly owned property of two debtors. Second, retain each matching specific subsection with its own amount: necessary wearing apparel under (a), a motor vehicle under (c), and a professionally prescribed health aid under uncapped (e).
Execution example: A hypothetical prescribed personal-use aid worth $3,000 receives both (b) at $3,000 and (e) at $3,000; hypothetical clothing likewise retains both (a) and (b).
by_task.avoid_when: Do not apply subsection (b) to business-use or nondebtor property, omit it because a specific subsection applies, or report its ceiling above the asset's value. Do not infer subsection (d) without stated trade use, and do not duplicate citations.

by_task.when: An asset matches an exemption's property and use category but the statute also states a dollar, aggregate, or item-count ceiling.
by_task.procedure: For EC, include the asset-law pairing if the law can protect any qualifying interest. Do not require the law to protect the asset's full value, and evaluate each asset as an eligible alternative rather than choosing a final allocation among competing assets.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not cite the law without the required property type, use, ownership, or other substantive eligibility facts; a ceiling cannot create category eligibility.

by_task.when: Considering a category-specific exemption rather than a general-property alternative.
by_task.procedure: Require the facts to satisfy that provision's stated property type and use. Federal § 522(d)(3) does not enumerate firearms; Arizona § 33-1125(1) and Pennsylvania § 8124(a)(1) require actual wearing apparel, not jewelry or firearms; Illinois § 12-1001(d) requires trade use and § 12-1001(e) requires a professionally prescribed health aid.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not transfer an exclusion to a different provision that expressly covers the item—for example, Oregon § 18.345(1)(b) expressly includes jewelry as well as wearing apparel. General-property alternatives remain independently available.

by_task.when: Arizona law applies to married debtors and Ariz. Rev. Stat. § 33-1121 is being considered for an asset.
by_task.procedure: Use § 33-1121 only to understand that spouses may claim and combine article exemptions; do not return it as the asset's exemption citation. Return the operative property provision whose category the asset satisfies.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not let this coordination rule remove an otherwise applicable Arizona property exemption or alter that provision's own married-couple limitation.

by_task.when: Pennsylvania exemptions are allowable and a category-specific exemption under 42 Pa. Cons. Stat. § 8124(a) is being considered for an asset.
by_task.procedure: Require the asset to match the cited category exactly. Section 8124(a)(1) applies only to actual wearing apparel and, because the supplied provision has no dollar ceiling, protects the whole asset value. Section 8124(a)(4) applies only to a commissioned officer's or enlisted person's uniform and accoutrements. The supplied § 8124(a) provisions do not create vehicle, jewelry, animal, furniture, or appliance exemptions. Evaluate § 8123 separately whenever applicable.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not treat jewelry, animals, vehicles, furniture, appliances, or other nonclothing property as wearing apparel, and do not copy the § 8123 ceiling into an uncapped § 8124(a)(1) claim.

by_task.when: Arizona exemptions are allowable and an asset is being evaluated under the supplied Arizona property provisions.
by_task.procedure: Return one claim only for each exact operative category the facts establish, using the lesser of whole-asset value and its stated ceiling. Section 33-1123 covers household furniture, furnishings, goods, electronics and appliances only when not otherwise specifically prescribed. Use § 33-1125(1) only for wearing apparel, (2) for musical instruments, (8) for one motor vehicle, (9) for a factually established prescribed prosthetic or medical aid, (10) for firearms, and (11) for domestic animals or household pets. Section 33-1125(4) is limited to engagement and wedding rings. Arizona's opt-out provision excludes federal § 522(d) alternatives.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not classify jewelry as apparel, extend the ring provision to other jewelry, treat a specifically listed instrument or apparel item as § 33-1123 property, cite coordination or heading provisions, add zero-value claims, duplicate claims, or include federal exemptions.

by_task.when: Oregon exemptions are allowable and debtor-owned personal property is household goods, furniture, a radio, television, or utensils held primarily for personal, family or household use.
by_task.procedure: Include Or. Rev. Stat. § 18.345(1)(f) as a category-specific alternative and report the lesser of the whole asset's value and $3,000. Evaluate paragraph (p), federal law and any other matching Oregon paragraph independently.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not omit paragraph (f) because paragraph (p) or a federal alternative also applies, and do not apply it to a vehicle, apparel, jewelry, or property outside its stated household category.

by_task.when: Wisconsin exemptions are allowable, the asset is a motor vehicle, and the case has one debtor.
by_task.procedure:
For each vehicle independently, include Wis. Stat. § 815.18(3)(g) and calculate its whole-asset claim in three steps: treat the $12,000 paragraph (d) capacity as unused unless the facts expressly establish another use; add it to the $4,000 motor-vehicle amount to obtain a $16,000 ceiling; then report the lesser of the vehicle's value and $16,000.
Execution example: A hypothetical vehicle worth $10,000 receives a § 815.18(3)(g) claim of $10,000; one worth $25,000 receives $16,000.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not stop at $4,000 when paragraph (d) capacity is unused, reduce that capacity by independently evaluated assets, exceed the vehicle's value, apply the provision to a nonvehicle, or infer a married-couple ceiling from this one-debtor rule.
